svg.title: The whole install, from an empty project to a locked-down GitLab — One interactive install builds the framework and configures GitLab
svg.text: The whole install, from an empty project to a
Scenario: One interactive install builds the framework and configures GitLab
Answer the questions, build the framework
The framework arrives as a merge request

g.text: Given a developer has just cloned a brand-new empty project into the
terminal
The empty copy (cloned from GitLab) as the developer sees it: git reports an empty project
with nothing saved yet. Set up off-screen: the test user, the installer, the tools it needs,
and the GitLab login.
When the developer starts the toolbox installer
The installer opens with its first question — install the complete framework? — with the
typed command still visible above it.
And the developer keeps the complete framework and the first question
asks about Ansible
Saying yes to the complete framework starts the setup questions from Copier (the tool that
builds the project from your answers); the first — does the project need Ansible? — defaults
to no.
And the developer keeps GitLab as the CI/CD platform
The next question asks which CI/CD platform to use — the automatic build-and-deploy system
that runs on every change; the developer keeps the default, GitLab.
And the developer keeps Docker as the container runtime
The next question asks which tool runs the containers; the developer keeps the default,
Docker.
And the developer keeps the generated docker-compose file
With Docker chosen, the setup offers to create project/docker-compose.yml; the developer
keeps the default, yes.
And the developer keeps the project workspace enabled
The next question turns the project workspace on or off (it adds project/Taskfile.yml and
docker-compose.yml); the developer keeps it on.
And the developer keeps Renovate auto-merge enabled
The next question asks whether Renovate — the bot that proposes dependency updates — should
merge toolbox updates on its own; the developer keeps it on.
And the developer keeps English as the Gherkin language
The last question sets the language for the test descriptions; the developer keeps the
default, en.
Then the installer builds the project and shows the finished screen
Answering the last question builds the framework and runs the setup all the way to the
finished screen.
And the project folder now holds the full DevSecOps framework
The project folder the questions produced: Taskfile.yml, .config, .gitlab-ci.yml, .agent and
more.
Then a merge request into main is now waiting for review on GitLab
The merge request from init-framework-devsecops into main, open and ready for review. The
framework never lands on main without this step.
And GitLab now lists main and the new init-framework-devsecops branch
GitLab's branches page: main, with the framework branch beside it.
Then GitLab now lets main accept only fast-forward merges
Main only accepts fast-forward merges: a branch must be up to date before it merges, so
history stays a straight line.
And GitLab now refuses pushes straight to main
On the protected-branches page: maintainers may merge, but no one may push straight to main.
Every change has to go through a review.
And GitLab now holds an automation token for the project
On the access-tokens page: TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN, with the Maintainer role. This is the
login the release automation uses.
And GitLab now keeps that token as a CI/CD variable
On the CI/CD variables page: the same token, saved as TASK_COMMITIZEN_TOKEN so the pipeline
can read it.
Then GitLab runs the whole framework pipeline and every stage passes
A runner is the machine that runs the pipeline (the checks GitLab runs on every change). The
embedded GitLab has a blank one waiting; this install points it at THIS project only, so it
runs the framework merge request's pipeline and steals no other. GitLab's own pipeline page
shows every job green.
And the framework merge request merges into main on its green pipeline
With the pipeline green, the merge request meets main's rule that a change may only merge
once its pipeline passes, so it merges. The merge request page now carries the Merged badge
— reached through review, never a forced push.
And main now carries the whole framework, merged through review
GitLab's file tree for main now holds the whole framework — Taskfile.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml,
.config, .agent — put there by a reviewed merge, not a direct push. The first install is
proven end to end.
